World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Exmouth residents displaced as town recovers from Cyclone Narelle
World.content:
Tahila Paul was just sitting down with a coffee on the couch with her husband when Cyclone Narelle ripped the roof off her home.

"We were here while the roof peeled off, and within seconds of the roof coming off, the water just started pouring through the downlights and the fans," she said.

"Minutes after that, the ceiling gyprock just started falling down.

"There was nothing you could do."

Tahila Paul had just renovated her home before Tropical Cyclone Narelle wreaked havoc. (ABC News: Kimberley Putland)

Cyclone Narelle impacted three states, and as it passed Exmouth in Western Australia, it was a category three in strength.

Tahila and her husband had purchased their home less than a year ago, and had all but finished renovating a week before the cyclone.

Weeks after Narelle, she stands in the gutted wreckage, with no certainty of when she will be able to return.

Tahila Paul and her partner are living with friends for now. (ABC Pilbara: Kimberley Putland)

"We're really lucky we've been able to stay at a friend's house for the next few weeks, but after that, to be honest, we haven't even really thought about it," she said.

"We're not sure — we have options to live with friends, so we are really lucky in that sense.

"I think it's going to come down to buying a caravan and living out the front in it.

"Because accommodation is tight in town and now trades are going to have to come into town, the town still needs tourism to come in."

Crisis point

While one-off disaster relief payments and energy bill relief from state and federal governments eased some of the financial burden, they did little to ease accommodation shortages.

Since the cyclone, Exmouth has struggled to welcome tourists with many expressing their frustrations.

However, out of more than 3,000 people who call Exmouth home, Ms Paul and her husband are not the only displaced locals struggling to find somewhere to stay.

Shire president Matt Niikkula said the housing crisis was something the shire was trying to address.

Matt Niikkula says housing in the town is at crisis point. (ABC News: Kimberley Putland)

"The lack of housing is affecting so many people and as insurance is moving through and displacing more and more locals … we're scrambling to try to find accommodation for teachers, essential workers," Mr Niikkula said.

"Housing is our biggest crisis point at the moment.

"Trying to get enough trades into town to be able to fix these houses, enough insurance assessors … the accommodation lacks spread right across, and it's something that we're trying as a council, as the shire, very hard to try to get a hold of.

Tropical Cyclone Narelle destroyed homes in Exmouth. (ABC Pilbara: Kimberley Putland)

"From a local government perspective, we're trying to take into account everyone's needs and wants, and it's not all just about the loudest screamers."

No homes to live in

Ray White Exmouth principal licensee Mark Lucas put a call out for homes on social media after clients and families he worked with were displaced.

He expected the crisis to get worse.

"We've probably seen that number doubled now to probably closer to 10 to 15 per cent of our portfolios that are unusable properties and people being displaced and looking for somewhere else to live," Mr Lucas said.

Homes in Exmouth were left uninhabitable after Cyclone Narelle. (ABC News: Kimberley Putland)

He said that number could keep increasing.

"It's still evolving, so we're still having insurance assessors come to town and saying that properties are uninhabitable — that's a daily occurrence now.

"Caravan parks are closed, national parks closed — there is nowhere for people to go."

Mark Lucas says the next plan for housing development needs to happen now. (ABC News: Kimberley Putland)

While Cyclone Narelle has further stressed the housing market, Mr Lucas said the problem stemmed from a lack of land releases, with the latest development — Sundrift — the first release in close to 20 years.

Mr Lucas said the new estate would provide some relief, but accommodation was still around 18 months away after titles were issued and houses built.

"I think what needs to happen, though, is that they need to be ready with the next [land release] after that," he said.

"You don't want to be going back to the very start of the investigation stage."

In a special council meeting in the weeks after Cyclone Narelle, the shire approved an overflow caravan park for self-contained caravans.

Mr Niikkula said the town had been amazing as it faced each challenge as part of the recovery from Cyclone Narelle.

"I think for me, the biggest takeaway is just the pride that I have in the town, in the community, of how we've all sort of come together and got through this as one," he said.

Tahila Paul agreed.

"The town's been amazing."

World.title: Senior classes arrive in remote outback town after 150 years
World.content:
Students in parts of outback Queensland will be given the chance to complete year 12 close to home for the first time.

People living in the Gulf of Carpentaria are used to isolation and going without essential services, with the nearest town a six-hour drive away.

And education has been no exception.

Towns in the Gulf of Carpentaria were isolated for up to four months from December due to flooding. (Supplied: Carpentaria Shire Council)

Between Mount Isa and Burketown, year 10 has been the highest level of schooling available.

Families have faced a difficult choice: send their children away or see them drop out.

But late last year, Gulf Christian College in Normanton purchased a TAFE building so it could start teaching senior classes for the first time in the town's 150-year history.

Year 10 was previously the highest education on offer across the region. (Supplied: Gulf Christian College)

'Leaving isn't an option'

Principal Andrew Evetts said the goal was to keep students with their families.

"If you wanted to go on to higher education in year 11, you had to leave and go to boarding school in Cairns, Townsville, Mount Isa or Brisbane," he said.

"Indigenous kids often have a hard time in boarding schools.

"The new classes are opening doors now for not just Normanton people but for Karumba, Croydon, places within a certain distance from us."

Andrew Evetts says students previously had to travel to Mount Isa, Townsville or Brisbane to finish schooling. (ABC News: Tim Little)

Boarding has long been part of life in regional Australia, but high costs and separation from country put it out of reach for many Gulf families.

"For the majority, it's not [an option]," he said.

"A lot of the parents want to keep their children here. This is their connection to where they belong and where they live, and leaving isn't an option for them."

The gap is reflected in the 2021 census, which showed 20 per cent of adults in Carpentaria Shire left school at year 10, compared with 10 per cent nationally.

End of a long goodbye

Blake Gregory, 17, is something of a celebrity in Normanton and will be one of the students graduating as part of the first year 12 cohort.

Blake Gregory is studying a certificate II while training for the Oceania Championships. (ABC News: Tim Little)

The rising decathlete recently placed seventh at the National Athletics Championships and has his sights set even higher.

"Every competition that I went to, I kept doing 13 events over two days, and they were all in the decathlon," he said.

"My next event is the Oceania Championships. I'm training to get on the Australian team for the next champs.

"Everyone in this town, they live for sports. But where we're from, there's hardly anywhere to do it."

Blake Gregory is part of the first graduating cohort from Gulf Christian College. (ABC News: Tim Little)

Later this year, Blake will join five other students graduating from the first locally taught year 12 classes.

Blake is also completing a certificate II in sport and recreation and has begun working with the local council.

New classes need everyone on board

Senior school coordinator and teacher Peter Lister said that for the more than 60 students enrolled in year 7 and above, senior classes brought structure and opportunity.

"School brings a lot of consistency and normalises having things on each week," he said.

"It's tough if you're the only hurdler in a town because you've got no competition and no-one to say, 'Hey, let's run, let's race'.

"Schools offer events and groups to compete with."

Peter Lister says senior classes bring structure and opportunity. (Supplied: Gulf Christian College)

The school is planning to expand the program, introducing ATAR subjects including physics and chemistry, along with more school-based traineeships.

Mr Evetts said the shift would be a generational change for the region, but one that needed the whole community to adapt.

"It's had some challenges. But it's about getting everyone on board to understand that year 11 is important, and if they don't attend regularly, if they're not at school, if they're not engaged, it makes year 12 just a waste of time," he said.

"When you're starting something new, it's not just new for the school, it's new for the community."

World.title: Cummins clips centurion Connolly as Aussies light up IPL
World.content:
Hyderabad Sunrisers captain Pat Cummins was man of the match as Punjab's Cooper Connolly joined the elite gang of IPL centurions in a losing cause.

Punjab Kings coach Ricky Ponting watched unimpressed as his side spilled a host of chances, helping the Sunrisers to leapfrog them to the top of the table with a 33-run victory at home.

Cummins had one of his Midas days, taking two key wickets (2-34), grabbing two challenging catches and making a series of canny decisions.

The only thing the Australian captain didn't win at the Rajiv Gandhi International Stadium was the toss, but put in to bat, he watched in glee as Travis Head thumped 38 off 19, Abhishek Sharma 35 off 13 and four glorious chances (three catches and one stumping) got bungled as his side amassed a formidable 4-235.

Connolly himself put down Ishan Kishan, spilling a simple one on the boundary edge off Lockie Ferguson when he'd scored just 9, while Heinrich Klaasen got dropped too in the deep for the same score by Shashank Singh off the luckless spinner Yuzvendra Chahal.

These proved expensive, as Kishan went on to hammer 55 off 32 and Klaasen 69 off 43.

Cummins showed Punjab how it should be done. After laying a nice trap and bouncing out Priyansh Arya in his opening over, he then held on to two awkward steepling catches under the lights as the Kings slumped to 3-23.

Hyderabad's win was almost done and dusted once Marcus Stoinis fell for a brisk 28 off 14 and Cummins (2-34) returned to get rid of Suryansh Shedge just as a fightback was being threatened.

But it turned into a lone show of resistance as Connolly hit eight sixes and seven fours to become Australia's 12th IPL centurion as wickets tumbled around him.

He reached his maiden hundred off 57 balls, another landmark in his exceptional debut season, in the final over, finishing on 107no in the Kings' 7-202.

AAP

World.title: Housing and cost-of-living relief at heart of WA budget
World.content:
The Western Australian government has foreshadowed a state budget with housing as the "number one priority", with targeted cost-of-living relief and health infrastructure also set to be key features.

Exactly how much money will be set aside to tackle each issue, and how much of it will help Western Australians, will be unveiled later today.

Mia John Toru hopes the budget will provide some relief. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

Single mother-of-five Mia John Toru has her fingers crossed this year's budget will help make her life a little easier.

Her biggest worry is how expensive it has become to keep a roof over her family's heads, especially after moving into a slightly larger home.

"I pay $730 a week, and that's almost, that's 48 per cent of my salary," she said.

Her landlord is looking to sell the home, and she is dreading having to foray back into the housing market as prices and the cost of renting continue to soar.

Mia John Toru pays almost half her salary in rent. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

"I think it's just going to keep going up," she said.

" I wish the government could give everyone a first home … you only need one home, so that you can call it your family home. "

A home for everyone is also an issue Premier Roger Cook has said he is working on.

Roger Cook has said that housing is a priority. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"My government's priority is to ensure every Western Australian has a place that they can call home," he said yesterday.

What's in this year's budget?

Several state budget measures have already been announced to tackle housing supply, including funds to build new homes for first-time buyers and regional workers, and additional social and affordable housing.

Mia John Toru wants the government to give everyone a first home. (ABC News: Peter Garnish)

The state government has flagged that targeted measures will remain its preferred way of tackling the cost of living, as opposed to broader measures.

One-off rent relief payments for people at risk of eviction will stick around, and free public transport on Sundays and for school students will become permanent.

Some measures yet to be announced include whether student assistance payments will be continued to help families with school expenses, and what relief measures will be made available for utility bills, such as water and electricity.

The treasurer will deliver the budget speech at parliament later today. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

Health infrastructure is also on the agenda, with an additional $1.5 billion set to go towards hospitals and beds; the state budget will reveal how much of this will go towards cost blowouts for existing projects.

Rising costs mean little savings

Like many Australians, Ms Toru is thrifty; she buys all her groceries and household needs in bulk, and does not spend much on luxuries like fast food.

But as her pay stretches thinner and thinner to keep up with rising costs, even affording necessities and building a savings account has become nearly impossible.

Mia John Toru working out her bills. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

"Before 2024, like, I was able to save some money, you know?" she said.

" But now, I can't afford to do some savings … I earn a decent income. Even a decent income can't save. "

Expenses like a gym membership have become luxuries, as food and fuel take up a growing chunk of her income.

"I put that [gym] on pause recently, only because diesel went up," she said.

"I need to cover the basics and the essentials, make sure our bills [are paid]."

Ms Toru wants to see cost-of-living relief in this year's budget, but also longer-term funding to meaningfully address the issues driving up those costs, such as housing supply.

"It's always good to get some relief, but I always say I think it's the wrong relief they're looking at."

She hopes this year she is the one who is wrong.

World.title: How high teas are helping break Mother's Day 'void'
World.content:
Jessica Rogers will never forget the day she had to leave hospital after giving birth, without her baby in her arms.

Warning: This content contains information and images relating to pregnancy loss and neonatal loss, which some readers might find distressing.

Her daughter Willow was stillborn at 24 weeks, after developing a tumour on her lung that was pressing on her heart.

"During the actual moment, it was all such a blur because so many emotions are going through your mind … just devastation," Ms Rogers said.

"We had about 24 hours … once we had birthed her, we got to hold her, and name her … and had time with our family so we could all grieve.

Jessica Rogers holding her stillborn baby Willow. (Supplied: Jessica Rogers)

" Leaving hospital without her wasn't something I ever thought I would have to experience. "

That was in 2017, and Ms Rogers's eldest child was four at the time.

Nearly a decade later, Ms Rogers is now a mother of three and said talking about Willow had been an important part of processing her grief.

Jessica Rogers with her husband and three sons, taking part in a Bears of Hope event. (Supplied: Jessica Rogers)

She is looking forward to sharing stories with others at an upcoming Mother's Day high tea run by the charity Bears of Hope for women who have experienced pregnancy and infant loss.

Ms Rogers is attending the event in Laurieton in northern New South Wales, which is one of 18 Bears of Hope high teas being held across Australia on May 9, the day before Mother's Day.

The events aim to provide a safe and nurturing environment for bereaved mums, at a time when they can feel isolated in their grief.

If a baby's name has been provided, it is featured on a place card, and mums also receive a keepsake gift.

A place card at a Windsor-based high tea. (Supplied: Bears of Hope)

"It's about bringing that community connection," Ms Rogers said.

" The event gives me a sense of belonging, which allows me to have a safe place to feel understood, and not judged for the way I grieve or how I feel. "

Abby Dante with a soft toy bear which is given to bereaved mums in hospitals to comfort the pain of leaving with empty arms. (ABC News: Emma Siossian)

Bears of Hope's Abby Dante has organised the Laurieton event and said it helped spark conversations.

"It brings a real awareness to the fact that it is much more common than people can begin to understand," she said.

" We like to recognise that all mums are mums, whether you are holding a baby in your arms or not. "

Breaking the silence

Jessica Rogers said they had time with their stillborn baby Willow, and captured some treasured photos. (Supplied: Jessica Rogers)

According to charity Red Nose Australia, about one in four confirmed pregnancies end in miscarriage or early pregnancy loss.

About 300,000 babies are born in Australia each year, and about 2,300 do not survive.

Jennifer Thomas is the Sydney-based Bears of Hope fundraising and events coordinator and became involved after her first son Bailey was stillborn 17 years ago.

Jennifer Thomas with her children. (Supplied: Jennifer Thomas)

She said the Mother's Day high tea event had grown steadily since it began 15 years ago.

"There's a void for mums once they have lost a baby," Ms Thomas said.

"There's this invisible silence, so this event is for those mums who might not be recognised as mums on Mother's Day.

" We have parents who have been attending for more than 10 years, and it's their one event in the year where they get to be acknowledged as their baby's mum. "

Place cards are used to acknowledge the name of babies after miscarriage or stillbirth. (Supplied: Bears of Hope)

Ms Thompson said bereaved women from older generations also attended.

"These are the women who were told in hospital rooms, 'There, there, you can try again,'" she said.

"And these mums are now getting the opportunity to be acknowledged, something they didn't all those years ago … they were that generation who didn't get to meet their baby."

Melbourne mother Fanoula Anasta started coordinating a Bears of Hope Mother's Day high tea event at Brunswick about four years ago, and said she saw many older women attend.

Fanoula Anasta says hosting a Mother's Day high tea event has helped her connect with other bereaved women and process her grief. (Supplied: Fanoula Anasta )

Ms Anasta was supported by Bears of Hope after she lost her baby Luke after going into pre-term labour at Melbourne's Frances Perry House hospital in 2021, and has two other children.

"Some of the women who come are in their 60s and their 70 …they say, 'In my day and age, we could never talk about it, thanks for talking about it,'" she said.

" In our culture, we are Greek; no-one ever spoke about it. It was like, 'we move on' …we do move on, but we need people to know about it. "

A Bears of Hope Mother's Day high tea at Narrabeen in Sydney. (Supplied: Bears of Hope)

Ms Anasta has fundraised extensively for Bears of Hope and said the high tea events had created long-term friendships.

She said she cried each time she gave a speech at a high tea event.

"The grief doesn't get better, it gets different," she said.

"I have found my healing through these other women I am helping.

"It is actually a beautiful afternoon with women sharing their stories about their beautiful babies … we are keeping our babies' legacy alive."

World.title: Live: ASX rebound set to continue as Wall Street's record rally rolls on
World.content:
Home building costs are set to jump between 4-to-12% in the coming year, and 20-thousand fewer residences built due to the impact of war related inflation, according to the CBA economics team.

In a reassessment of the outlook for housing construction costs and supply, CBA says higher diesel, freight and petrochemical costs are now flowing through to construction costs, with a wave of supplier notices and fuel surcharges landing from April.

“The central estimate is that the war adds 4.0%to aggregate dwelling input costs over the coming year, relative to the pre-war path,” CBA says. “As a result, we expect new construction output price growth to peak around 8% by Q3 2026.”

CBA’s “downside” scenario where the war drags on for longer and the impacts are higher home building costs could rise by 12% “at its peak”.

The bank points out, as costs rise fewer projects are feasible, and the financial incentive to build weakens.

“Relative to our pre-war baseline, we estimate around 15,000 fewer dwellings will be built by late-2029as a result of higher construction costs. “In the downside scenario, the shortfall rises to around 25,000 dwellings.”

CBA found the most immediate cost pressures are concentrated in plastics and freight-linked categories, including PVC and fuel-related surcharges on concrete deliveries.

“April and May 2026 mark the initial escalation phase for input prices, with the average announced price increase from plumbing and trade suppliers rising to 11% in April and May, from around 5% in the months prior to the Iran war.”

CBA warns that even if the conflict stabilises, cost growth could take some time to slow, and it doesn’t expect the high prices to unwind.

“Supply chains take time to normalise, inventories need to be rebuilt, and backlogs must be cleared. “Builders and suppliers may also continue to price conservatively to compensate for ongoing project risk.”

World.title: Live: Tony Abbott positions to become next Liberal Party president
World.content:
The federal government has committed to looking at developing a national early education and care commission, which the education minister says could further strengthen safety in the sector.

The Productivity Commission was asked by the government in 2023 to examine the prospect of universal childcare, with the report finalised in 2024.

It recommended that the child care subsidy should be modified, but it did not back a 90 per cent subsidy for all families.

It also recommended federal and state governments should establish an independent early education commission.

The report suggested the commission could monitor the progress of government policies and programs in the sector and provide independent advice on how to ensure the best outcomes.

Nearly two years after the report was finalised, Education Minister Jason Clare has confirmed that federal and state governments will consult with service providers, unions, peak bodies and other stakeholders about the design of the potential commission.

"This is the next potential step to drive long-term reform," he said.

It's expected that the federal government will report back to state education ministers with the next steps by either the end of this year or early next year.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has previously said he wants universal childcare to be his legacy, but the details of how such a scheme would work or when it would come into place remain unclear.

World.title: Can the budget soothe sleepless Victorian voters as cost of living rises?
World.content:
Maybe you wake up in the middle of the night, worried about your mortgage.

Maybe, like one texter to 774 ABC Melbourne, you "live pay cheque to pay cheque".

So, does the Victorian treasurer wake up worried about the state's debt?

"That's a great question. I have a lot of sleepless nights," Jaclyn Symes said.

" Would I prefer debt to be lower? Of course. "

For the first time since COVID, Victoria is spending less than it earns. But that's if you count what's called an "operating surplus".

Add spending on big projects and building new schools, and each year the budget is in the red.

Loading Instagram content

Add up all those annual deficits, and the bill on the debt is mounting rapidly.

When Labor was last elected in 2022, the debt cost, or the annual interest bill, was $4 billion.

It's already doubled and will triple to $11.8 billion by the end of the decade.

That's more than enough to keep a treasurer up at night.

It means that one dollar in every 10 spent by the Victorian government will not go towards police or hospitals. It will instead be used to pay off debt.

Over 12 years, the Coalition and many media figures have tried to turn debt into an electoral weapon to use against Labor.

It hasn't worked.

The Coalition is hoping that debt will finally change votes, and the government is worried it could.

However, that "operating surplus" in the budget is not aimed at voters as much as it is aimed at the ratings agencies that set the price of debt.

"I'm hoping [the operating surplus] gets us through the ratings agencies," one senior government figure told me.

There are voters furious with this government. And Labor's poll numbers are poor — lower than at the last election.

Are the handouts worth it?

There are good reasons why a listener like Sue texts 774 to say: "OMG, please don't stop the handouts, we are hurting!"

Here's why.

The state budget landed on the same day the Reserve Bank once again jacked up interest rates.

It means that since Christmas, homeowners are paying $272 extra per month on a $600,000 mortgage.

It's one reason the treasurer's budget will give back each household $176 on their car rego.

If you add in the discounts on public transport in Victoria, then maybe the state government will have given voters what the Reserve Bank has taken away.

Victorians are being offered free public transport to help with rising cost-of-living pressures. (AAP: Tracey Nearmy)

It's exactly what keeps voters awake or sends them to sleep in tears.

Rod rang in from Cranbourne to say: "I had my daughter in tears last night after hearing the interest rates going up … she could lose her house."

However, handouts like the rego rebate are exactly what worries Reserve Bank Governor Michele Bullock.

Such handouts made it "harder to dampen demand", she said.

In central bank language, she is saying the handouts lead to inflation, which leads to another rate hike, which could cancel out the handout.

Voters are not just angry at politicians; they're angry at institutions like the Reserve Bank.

Michele Bullock also sounds like someone who is not sleeping well.

RBA governor Michele Bullock says initiatives being offered by the Victorian government could feed inflation. (ABC News: Nick Haggarty)

The bank thinks it has no choice but to raise rates.

"We are poorer, and there is no way out of that," Bullock said, "and the trade-off is much worse."

But to some, it feels like needless punishment.

Deb, who is a mortgage broker in the Macedon Ranges, told 774: "Everyone, your average battler, medium income family, they're struggling week to week."

When asked, "Do you think the Reserve Bank understands that?" Deb answered, "No, I don't."

Can all these sleepless nights lead the Liberal Party to victory?

If treasurers, Reserve Bank governors and voters are having sleepless nights, can the Liberals turn that into an electoral victory?

Anger may not be enough.

The Liberal Party has won only one state election in the past 30 years.

Jess Wilson is a first-term MP. She is both shadow treasurer and opposition leader, and she leads a party with a poor track record of being nice to each other.

She has her fair share of sleepless nights.

If she wants to wield debt as a political weapon, she has to convince voters she has a plan.

Opposition leader Jess Wilson campaigning with Anthony Marsh during the Nepean by-election. (ABC News)

She's made some announcements, but none can be shown to significantly rein in spending, let alone pay down a big chunk of debt.

Wilson says voters are "looking for politicians to stop spinning their way out of the mess that they have created".

The Liberals have held contradictory positions on the state's biggest project.

The Coalition opposes the $35 billion Suburban Rail Loop (SRL), but it's not clear whether its multiple contracts can be stopped. About $7 billion has already been spent, and tunnelling will have begun before the election.

How do you "untunnel" a tunnel?

Wilson plans to pause the SRL, but will that end up costing billions more?

"We will do the responsible and commonsense thing by the taxpayer," she says.

To win in November, Jess Wilson needs a record shift in voter sentiment, and you don't get credit for having sleepless nights.

As Steven rang in to tell 774: "I haven't had a pay rise in six years. I know mates who are selling houses to try to downsize. It's hard out there at the moment."

When voters wake up on the final Saturday in November, they will go with the party that understands that pain.

World.title: How a YouTube video of Cathy Freeman led a 14-year-old to the Commonwealth Games
World.content:
SportAthleticsCommonwealth Games How a YouTube video of Cathy Freeman led a 14-year-old to the Commonwealth Games Frances Howe May 7, 2026 — 8:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Lexie Brown first learned who Cathy Freeman was, she thought she’d been let in on a secret. Brown was born a tick over a decade after Freeman won gold in the 400m at the Sydney 2000 Olympics. So it wasn’t until she was six and the 2016 Rio Games were on TV that Freeman was first brought up into the conversation by her nan, Wendy. Lexi Brown will make her Commonwealth Games debut at just 14-years-old. Casey Sims for Australian Athletics Wendy explained that Freeman was a sprinter, just like her granddaughter, and switched off the Rio Games to instead search YouTube for a replay of Freeman’s sprint. “She probably was the first-ever athlete I watched get a medal for Australia,” Brown, now 14, said. “And her being Aboriginal was another big thing because I’m Aboriginal, on my dad’s side I’m from the Kamilaroi in Moree and on my mum’s side, I’m Gumbaynggirr from around Nambucca. Watching her achieve that much as an Aboriginal woman, it made me feel so good about being Aboriginal.”



It wouldn’t be until years later, after coming face-to-face with several statues of Freeman, that Brown figured her secret was out. “As a little kid, you think every big thing you see is your little secret, until you realise other people know about it too,” she said. “I watched her 400m so many times … I can’t count – I’ve seen it so many times and I still watch it to this day.” In watching that video as many times as she has, Brown has started to mimic it. On Thursday, she was named in Australia’s para athletics squad for the 2026 Commonwealth Games to be held in Glasgow from July. At 14, she’ll be running against women more than twice her age. Lexi Brown competing at the 2026 World Para Athletics Championships in New Delhi, India. Australian Athletics Brown, who was born without most of the lower limb of her left arm, made her international debut at the 2025 Para World Championships in New Delhi, achieving a personal best in the 100m and a bronze medal and Australian record in the universal 4x100m relay.



Although it was a great year for Brown’s career, it was also one marred by loss after the death of her nan in January. Her medal and certificate from the competition sit on display in the lounge room next to the TV that once showed the Rio Games and next to her nan’s ashes. “The tears were also a very immediate thing,” Brown said of the moments after her international debut. “For my first international comp I was really excited for my nan to be there with me because she was my biggest supporter ever. And she probably is from heaven and I keep that in my heart.” Brown will compete in Glasgow with a new prosthetic which helps steady her on the starting blocks and propel her body when she runs. The teenager will also head to Glasgow with some advice from her idol, Freeman, who she met at a track meet in Melbourne in March. “As soon as I saw her, I thought ‘is that Cathy? World.content:
Low-level snow has fallen early on Thursday, which is set to be Victoria’s coldest day of the year, as a cold front sweeps across south-eastern Australia.

The Bureau of Meteorology said at least several centimetres of snow had already blanketed all Victorian alpine resorts, and that snow was expected to fall in parts of the state with elevations of 600 metres.

The temperature is set to reach a top of 14 degrees in Melbourne on Thursday. Paul Jeffers

The plunging temperatures have been brought on by a blast of cold winds from the Southern Ocean, which collided with a cloud bank over south-eastern Australia and caused rain. In elevated parts of Victoria where there is enough cool air close to the ground, the rain will fall as snow.

“Because this was a fairly brief burst of cold air ... the snow level is going up today, so it was down to 600 metres but it will be rising [in elevation] pretty quickly over the course of the day,” said bureau meteorologist Robert Urbaniak.

The Sheep Detectives adds a new dimension to the cosy crime genre. It also redefines the term “woolly headed”. In this murder story, the crime is solved by a flock of sheep whose powers of deduction rival Miss Marple’s.

The film is a rather loose adaptation of Three Bags Full, a 2005 bestseller originally written in German but set in an Irish village. Its author uses the pseudonym Leonie Swann, preferring to keep her real name secret even though the book has been translated into 26 languages, as well as prompting a follow-up.

Hugh Jackman as George Hardy in The Sheep Detectives. Courtesy of Amazon MGM Studios

The screen version, however, is quintessentially English. Its human characters are variations on the types who have populated countless British sitcoms. The only exotics are the sheep themselves – a diverse selection of breeds who come across as such fierce individualists that the word “sheep-like” becomes as redundant as “woolly headed”.

The other surprise is the identity of the victim – Hugh Jackman, cast as the flock’s shepherd, George Hardy, whose early demise means that Jackman is largely seen in flashback. A vegetarian who detests the butcher, he regards his sheep as his best friends, relaxing every evening by reading them crime stories. On these occasions, Lily, a light-brown Shetland voiced by Julia Louis-Dreyfus, usually manages to guess the culprit – a skill that will prove invaluable in the days ahead.

World.title: ‘Mouth of the South’: Billionaire CNN founder Ted Turner dies
World.content:
Updated BusinessCompaniesVale ‘Mouth of the South’: Billionaire CNN founder Ted Turner dies David Bauder Updated May 7, 2026 — 6:45am ,first published 5:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ted Turner, the outspoken television pioneer who created a media empire and transformed the news business by creating CNN and introducing the 24-hour cable news cycle, has died aged 87. The father of five died on Wednesday surrounded by his family, according to Turner Enterprises, the company that oversees his vast business interests and investments. Jane Fonda and Ted Turner, who were married from 1991 to 2001, pose together at an event in 2013. AP Turner’s empire expanded far beyond media – owning professional sports teams in Atlanta and huge chunks of the American West. He raced yachts too, defending the America’s Cup in 1977. He donated a stunning $US1 billion ($1.4 billion) to United Nations charities and fuelled conservation efforts.



Turner married three women – most famously actor Jane Fonda – and earned the nicknames “Captain Outrageous” and “The Mouth of the South.” Related Article Updated

Media & marketing James Murdoch makes $418m offer for US media assets: report He once bragged: “If only I had a little humility, I’d be perfect.” He was slowed in later years by Lewy body dementia. Long since out of the television business, he concentrated on philanthropy. His garrulous personality sometimes overshadowed a driven, risk-taking business acumen. By the time he sold his Turner Broadcasting System to Time Warner Inc. in a 1996 media megadeal, Turner had turned his late father’s billboard company into a global conglomerate that included seven major cable networks, three professional sports teams and a pair of hit movie studios.



US President Donald Trump, reacting to Turner’s death, called him “one of the Greats of All Time.” “Whenever I needed him, he was there, always willing to fight for a good cause!” Trump posted on social media. Turner’s signature achievement was creating the Cable News Network (CNN), the first 24-hour, all-news television network in 1980. AP The president also took aim at the current owners of the network, saying they had “destroyed Turner’s baby” and saying he hoped its next owners will be able to “bring it back to its former glory and credibility”. CNN is set to change hands again soon, with Trump supporter David Ellison’s Paramount Skydance reaching a deal to acquire CNN’s parent company Warner Bros earlier this year. CNN’s chief international anchor Christian Amanpour, who has been at the network since 1983, paid tribute to Turner.



“Remember when giants strode the world? Ted Turner was a giant,” she said. “He said it like it was and like it is, and we were his willing foot soldiers. And I think he changed not just the world, but all of our lives, too.” Turner’s signature achievement was creating the Cable News Network (CNN), the first 24-hour, all-news television network in 1980. View post on X In part, Turner’s own frustration with television news was the instigator. He often worked past 8pm, after the ABC, CBS and NBC nightly newscasts had already gone off the air.



He took a chance by starting the operation in the early days of cable television, living in an apartment above its Atlanta office. CNN’s breakthrough moment came during the Gulf War with Iraq in 1991. Most television journalists had fled Baghdad, but CNN stayed, capturing arresting images of a war’s outbreak. Loading Turner was promised a continued role in CNN after his company’s sale to Time Warner but was gradually pushed out, much to his regret. “The mistake I made was losing control of the company,” he later said.



Turner’s rise from uni dropout to media mogul Robert Edward Turner III was born November 19, 1938, in Cincinnati. When he was nine, his family moved to Savannah, Georgia, where he grew up. After being expelled from Brown University, Turner came to Atlanta to work for his domineering father’s billboard company, Turner Advertising. After his father’s 1963 suicide, Turner took over the company. In 1970, he bought an independent UHF station with a weak signal that didn’t even cover Atlanta. Ted Turner is seen at his desk inside the CNN Centre in 1982. AP On December 17, 1976, he began transmitting the station to cable systems across the country via satellite. It became the TBS SuperStation.



TBS’ motley collection of old movies and sitcom reruns was augmented by Turner’s acquisition of baseball’s Atlanta Braves. Perennial doormats, the Braves slowly attracted fans nationwide through their superstation exposure. In the 1980s, Turner went deeply into debt to buy MGM, a move again greeted with scepticism. But the acquisition gave his company a library of vintage movies that eventually were parlayed into the TNT and Turner Classic Movies networks. ‘The mistake I made was losing control of the company.’ Ted Turner He revealed his ambitions as a younger man: “I used to tell people I wanted to become the world’s greatest sailor, businessman and lover all at the same time.” For much of his life a partying roustabout who wooed beautiful women, the lean, mustachioed sportsman married three times. He was married to Fonda from 1991 to 2001. She tired of his philandering and divorced him, although they remained friends.



Perhaps Turner’s greatest love was for the land. He acquired millions of acres in ranches complete with roaming buffalo and was Nebraska’s largest private landholder. Researchers at Texas A&M University credited his donation of a few bulls in 2005 with helping increase the genetic diversity of the last herd of southern Plains bison. Related Article Vale ‘It was beautiful’: In his last hours, James Valentine delivered one final performance He had a net worth of $US2.5 billion in 2023 but had dropped off Forbes magazine’s ranking of the 400 richest Americans in 2021. “See, my life is more an adventure than a quest to make money,” Turner once said. Turner managed to insult many with his shoot-from-the-lip style. An atheist since his only sister died of lupus at age 17, he called Christians “losers” and “Jesus freaks,” later apologising for both remarks.



Turner grabbed a leadership role in American philanthropy with his 1997 pledge to give $US1 billion to UN charities. He joined former US Senator Sam Nunn to start the Nuclear Threat Initiative, a US-based nonprofit dedicated to reducing the threat of nuclear, biological and chemical weapons. World.title: ASX set to jump as oil falls and sharemarkets rally; AI giants surge
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to jump as oil falls and sharemarkets rally; AI giants surge Stan Choe Updated May 7, 2026 — 6:44am ,first published 5:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Oil prices sank, and stock markets rallied worldwide with hopes that the United States and Iran are nearing a deal to allow ships to deliver crude from the Persian Gulf once again to their customers. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil, the international standard, fell 7.8 per cent to $US101.27, down from more than $US115 early this week. It dropped as President Donald Trump said the Strait of Hormuz could be “OPEN TO ALL” if Iran accepts a reported agreement that the US president did not detail. Stocks around the world bounced higher and oil tumbled. AP The small strait has caused big trouble for the global economy because the war with Iran has blocked oil tankers from using it to exit the Persian Gulf. A reopening could allow oil to flow freely again and remove upward pressure on inflation that’s driving prices up for all kinds of products worldwide. On Wall Street, the S&P 500 climbed 1.5 per cent for its best day in nearly a month and hit another all-time high. The Dow Jones jumped 612 points, or 1.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite rose 2 per cent to its own record. The Australian sharemarket is set to jump, with futures at 4.54am AEST pointing to a jump of 105 points, or 1.2 per cent, at the open. The ASX surged by 1.3 per cent on Wednesday. The Australian dollar jumped and is trading at US72.40¢.



Related Article Dating Tinder boasts of astrology-led revival as singles events flourish Stock markets abroad had even bigger gains, with indexes leaping 6.5 per cent in Seoul, 2.9 per cent in Paris and 2.1 per cent in London. Of course, hopes have risen several times already on Wall Street about a possible end to the war with Iran, only to get dashed each time. That could happen again, and oil prices pared some of their steepest losses from Wednesday morning. The price for a barrel of Brent briefly dove below $97 before returning above $100 after Trump threatened to start bombing “at a much higher level and intensity” if Iran does not accept the agreement. Wall Street nevertheless latched onto some potentially encouraging signals. Trump said Tuesday he was pausing his effort to forcefully reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial ships. And China’s foreign minister called for a comprehensive ceasefire following a meeting with Iran’s foreign minister. That could be influential because of how closely tied Iran is to China economically and politically.



In the meantime, big US companies continue to turn in much stronger profits for the start of 2026 than analysts expected. That’s supporting the stock market despite all the uncertainties created by the war. AMD helped lead the market with a surge of 18.6 per cent after it joined the list of big-name companies topping expectations for both profit and revenue. CEO Lisa Su said the chip company benefited from continued growth from artificial-intelligence technology, which is demanding tremendous amounts of computing power from data centers. AMD also said its revenue growth could accelerate in the current quarter to roughly 46 per cent from a year earlier. Another company enmeshed in the AI industry, Super Micro Computer, rallied 24.5 per cent after likewise delivering stronger earnings than analysts expected. Nvidia, the chip company that became the poster child of the AI boom, rose 5.7 per cent and was the single strongest force lifting the S&P 500 because of its immense size. CVS Health climbed 7.6 per cent after delivering better results for the first quarter than analysts expected and raising its financial forecasts for the full year. Disney gained 7.5 per cent after saying its “Zootopia 2” movie helped draw people to its streaming business, parks and cruise ships, while delivering a better-than-expected profit. Uber Technologies drove 8.5 per cent higher after giving a bookings forecast for the spring that was higher than analysts expected.



Outside of earnings reports, companies with big fuel bills jumped on hopes that oil prices will continue to ease. That included gains of 6.8 per cent for United Airlines, 6.8 per cent for Carnival and 8.8 per cent for Royal Caribbean. Related Article Opinion

AI Trump goes ‘woke’ with a sudden change of mind Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist All told, the S&P 500 rose 105.90 points to 7,365.12. The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 612.34 to 49,910.59, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 512.82 to 25,838.94. In the bond market, Treasury yields sank as falling oil prices took pressure off inflation. The yield on the 10-year Treasury dropped to 4.35 per cent from 4.43 per cent late Tuesday. That’s a notable move for the bond market. Lower yields can bring down rates for mortgages and other kinds of loans going to US households and businesses, which in turn can give the economy a boost. Lower yields also tend to push upward on prices for stocks and other kinds of investments. The 10-year yield, though, remains well above its 3.97 per cent level from just before the war.



In stock markets abroad, South Korea’s Kospi jumped above the 7,000 level for the first time to a record thanks to big gains for AI winners, including Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: ‘People haven’t seen Chinese cuisine in such a way’: Mott 32 is coming to Melbourne
World.content:
Exclusive Eating outComing soon ‘People haven’t seen Chinese cuisine in such a way’: Mott 32 is coming to Melbourne Elaborate ceilings, luxe ingredients and tableside flair have won over fans around the world. For its Australian debut, it’s picked a flashy spot in Melbourne. Dani Valent May 7, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Is Melbourne ready for Peking duck aged for 42 days and smoked over applewood? That’s the signature dish at Hong Kong-born restaurant Mott 32, which will open its first Australian outlet at Crown Melbourne in March 2027 as part of the casino business’s $200 million shake-up of the riverside megaplex. Known for serving upscale Chinese food in swank settings, Mott 32 will slot into the site previously occupied by Silks, which closed in March. Inside Mott 32's clubby Hong Kong dining room. Named after the address of the first Chinese grocery in New York (32 Mott Street), the brand launched in 2014 in a bank tower in Hong Kong’s Central neighbourhood. There are now nine around the world, including Vancouver, Dubai and Las Vegas, with a pipeline of nine more locations including other Australian cities. Mott 32’s parent company Maximal Concepts was co-founded by entrepreneur, filmmaker and extreme sports adventurer Malcolm Wood.



“Melbourne’s a great city,” he says in the first interview he’s done about the push into Australia. “You’ve got a lot of tourism coming through, you’re multicultural, there’s a large Asian community, and you’re very well-educated about food – let’s call it culinary intelligence.” Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Even so, he believes Mott 32 will be something new for the city. “People haven’t seen Chinese cuisine presented in such a way, with a beautiful design that competes against all the other restaurants in the city.” The restaurant ages duck for 42 days before smoking and roasting each bird. Excellent cocktails, glamorous clubby design and theatrical flourishes are Mott 32 signatures, as are modern and technically challenging versions of Chinese classics. Siu mai dumplings are made with truffled Iberico pork and soft-boiled quail egg. That smoked, roasted duck (used across several dishes) is known for its glossy, crunchy skin and tableside carving. Born in Taiwan to a Chinese mother and English father, Wood is keen to differentiate Mott 32 from other international luxury brands such as Nobu (a Crown tenant since 2007) and Zuma, with more than 30 locations worldwide. Both serve Asian cuisine but were founded in New York and London, respectively.



“We pride ourselves in being from Asia,” says Wood. “And we are one of the few international restaurants in our segment that you’ll find Asian consumers wanting to go to.” Wood’s films focus on environmental challenges. The Last Glacier is about climate change, A Plastic Ocean investigates waste. How does he parlay that into a global hospitality business? “We teach ourselves about a problem, we drive awareness through a film, and then we try to change our business off the back of it,” he says. An artist's illustration of the entry to the Melbourne restaurant. He points to an egg initiative in Hong Kong, whereby the business set up its own cage-free organic egg farm that runs off solar to avoid having to import such eggs from Europe. “[Now] we’re one of the largest suppliers of eggs in Hong Kong.” At the same time, he admits hospitality has a long way to go.

World.title: How a YouTube video of Cathy Freeman led a 14-year-old to the Commonwealth Games
World.content:
SportAthleticsCommonwealth Games How a YouTube video of Cathy Freeman led a 14-year-old to the Commonwealth Games Frances Howe May 7, 2026 — 8:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Lexie Brown first learned who Cathy Freeman was, she thought she’d been let in on a secret. Brown was born a tick over a decade after Freeman won gold in the 400m at the Sydney 2000 Olympics. So it wasn’t until she was six and the 2016 Rio Games were on TV that Freeman was first brought up into the conversation by her nan, Wendy. Lexi Brown will make her Commonwealth Games debut at just 14-years-old. Casey Sims for Australian Athletics Wendy explained that Freeman was a sprinter, just like her granddaughter, and switched off the Rio Games to instead search YouTube for a replay of Freeman’s sprint. “She probably was the first-ever athlete I watched get a medal for Australia,” Brown, now 14, said. “And her being Aboriginal was another big thing because I’m Aboriginal, on my dad’s side I’m from the Kamilaroi in Moree and on my mum’s side, I’m Gumbaynggirr from around Nambucca. Watching her achieve that much as an Aboriginal woman, it made me feel so good about being Aboriginal.”



It wouldn’t be until years later, after coming face-to-face with several statues of Freeman, that Brown figured her secret was out. “As a little kid, you think every big thing you see is your little secret, until you realise other people know about it too,” she said. “I watched her 400m so many times … I can’t count – I’ve seen it so many times and I still watch it to this day.” In watching that video as many times as she has, Brown has started to mimic it. On Thursday, she was named in Australia’s para athletics squad for the 2026 Commonwealth Games to be held in Glasgow from July. At 14, she’ll be running against women more than twice her age. Lexi Brown competing at the 2026 World Para Athletics Championships in New Delhi, India. Australian Athletics Brown, who was born without most of the lower limb of her left arm, made her international debut at the 2025 Para World Championships in New Delhi, achieving a personal best in the 100m and a bronze medal and Australian record in the universal 4x100m relay.



Although it was a great year for Brown’s career, it was also one marred by loss after the death of her nan in January. Her medal and certificate from the competition sit on display in the lounge room next to the TV that once showed the Rio Games and next to her nan’s ashes. “The tears were also a very immediate thing,” Brown said of the moments after her international debut. “For my first international comp I was really excited for my nan to be there with me because she was my biggest supporter ever. And she probably is from heaven and I keep that in my heart.” Brown will compete in Glasgow with a new prosthetic which helps steady her on the starting blocks and propel her body when she runs. The teenager will also head to Glasgow with some advice from her idol, Freeman, who she met at a track meet in Melbourne in March. “As soon as I saw her, I thought ‘is that Cathy? Is that Cathy Freeman?’ ” Brown said. “I was probably kind of staring, I was like ‘this is a person I’ve watched so many times and that’s them right in front of me’.”



“Once we started talking, my nerves went. And you’d think seeing somebody as greater as her, you’d freeze up on the spot. But I was talking like it was another family member.” Related Article Commonwealth Games McEvoy won’t rule out shock relay return as Dolphins chase magic of Sydney 2000 in LA “She talked to me and another athlete Briseis [Brittain] through how she felt during [the Olympics] and how nerves are normal and how beautiful the crowds are at such a big event and I loved hearing her thoughts.” But even though she’s been told the nerves are normal, that hasn’t deterred them ahead of Glasgow. “I’ve had multiple dreams of different things … I’ve thought I’d get off the plane just freezing or being in that call room, freezing too. All of my thoughts have been freezing,” she said.



“A medal definitely is a big stretch, but dreams can go as far as they want.”

An atheist since his only sister died of lupus at age 17, he called Christians “losers” and “Jesus freaks,” later apologising for both remarks.



Turner grabbed a leadership role in American philanthropy with his 1997 pledge to give $US1 billion to UN charities. He joined former US Senator Sam Nunn to start the Nuclear Threat Initiative, a US-based nonprofit dedicated to reducing the threat of nuclear, biological and chemical weapons. World.title: ASX set to jump as oil falls and sharemarkets rally; AI giants surge
World.content:
BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to jump as oil falls and sharemarkets rally; AI giants surge Stan Choe Updated May 7, 2026 — 6:44am ,first published 5:15am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Oil prices sank, and stock markets rallied worldwide with hopes that the United States and Iran are nearing a deal to allow ships to deliver crude from the Persian Gulf once again to their customers. The price for a barrel of Brent crude oil, the international standard, fell 7.8 per cent to $US101.27, down from more than $US115 early this week. It dropped as President Donald Trump said the Strait of Hormuz could be “OPEN TO ALL” if Iran accepts a reported agreement that the US president did not detail. Stocks around the world bounced higher and oil tumbled. AP The small strait has caused big trouble for the global economy because the war with Iran has blocked oil tankers from using it to exit the Persian Gulf. A reopening could allow oil to flow freely again and remove upward pressure on inflation that’s driving prices up for all kinds of products worldwide. On Wall Street, the S&P 500 climbed 1.5 per cent for its best day in nearly a month and hit another all-time high. The Dow Jones jumped 612 points, or 1.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite rose 2 per cent to its own record. The Australian sharemarket is set to jump, with futures at 4.54am AEST pointing to a jump of 105 points, or 1.2 per cent, at the open. The ASX surged by 1.3 per cent on Wednesday. The Australian dollar jumped and is trading at US72.40¢.



Related Article Dating Tinder boasts of astrology-led revival as singles events flourish Stock markets abroad had even bigger gains, with indexes leaping 6.5 per cent in Seoul, 2.9 per cent in Paris and 2.1 per cent in London. Of course, hopes have risen several times already on Wall Street about a possible end to the war with Iran, only to get dashed each time. That could happen again, and oil prices pared some of their steepest losses from Wednesday morning. The price for a barrel of Brent briefly dove below $97 before returning above $100 after Trump threatened to start bombing “at a much higher level and intensity” if Iran does not accept the agreement. Wall Street nevertheless latched onto some potentially encouraging signals. Trump said Tuesday he was pausing his effort to forcefully reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial ships. And China’s foreign minister called for a comprehensive ceasefire following a meeting with Iran’s foreign minister. That could be influential because of how closely tied Iran is to China economically and politically.



In the meantime, big US companies continue to turn in much stronger profits for the start of 2026 than analysts expected. That’s supporting the stock market despite all the uncertainties created by the war. AMD helped lead the market with a surge of 18.6 per cent after it joined the list of big-name companies topping expectations for both profit and revenue. CEO Lisa Su said the chip company benefited from continued growth from artificial-intelligence technology, which is demanding tremendous amounts of computing power from data centers. AMD also said its revenue growth could accelerate in the current quarter to roughly 46 per cent from a year earlier. Another company enmeshed in the AI industry, Super Micro Computer, rallied 24.5 per cent after likewise delivering stronger earnings than analysts expected. Nvidia, the chip company that became the poster child of the AI boom, rose 5.7 per cent and was the single strongest force lifting the S&P 500 because of its immense size. CVS Health climbed 7.6 per cent after delivering better results for the first quarter than analysts expected and raising its financial forecasts for the full year. Disney gained 7.5 per cent after saying its “Zootopia 2” movie helped draw people to its streaming business, parks and cruise ships, while delivering a better-than-expected profit. Uber Technologies drove 8.5 per cent higher after giving a bookings forecast for the spring that was higher than analysts expected.



Outside of earnings reports, companies with big fuel bills jumped on hopes that oil prices will continue to ease. That included gains of 6.8 per cent for United Airlines, 6.8 per cent for Carnival and 8.8 per cent for Royal Caribbean. Related Article Opinion

AI Trump goes ‘woke’ with a sudden change of mind Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist All told, the S&P 500 rose 105.90 points to 7,365.12. The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 612.34 to 49,910.59, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 512.82 to 25,838.94. In the bond market, Treasury yields sank as falling oil prices took pressure off inflation. The yield on the 10-year Treasury dropped to 4.35 per cent from 4.43 per cent late Tuesday. That’s a notable move for the bond market. Lower yields can bring down rates for mortgages and other kinds of loans going to US households and businesses, which in turn can give the economy a boost. Lower yields also tend to push upward on prices for stocks and other kinds of investments. The 10-year yield, though, remains well above its 3.97 per cent level from just before the war.



In stock markets abroad, South Korea’s Kospi jumped above the 7,000 level for the first time to a record thanks to big gains for AI winners, including Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: ‘People haven’t seen Chinese cuisine in such a way’: Mott 32 is coming to Melbourne
World.content:
Exclusive Eating outComing soon ‘People haven’t seen Chinese cuisine in such a way’: Mott 32 is coming to Melbourne Elaborate ceilings, luxe ingredients and tableside flair have won over fans around the world. For its Australian debut, it’s picked a flashy spot in Melbourne. Dani Valent May 7, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Is Melbourne ready for Peking duck aged for 42 days and smoked over applewood? That’s the signature dish at Hong Kong-born restaurant Mott 32, which will open its first Australian outlet at Crown Melbourne in March 2027 as part of the casino business’s $200 million shake-up of the riverside megaplex. Known for serving upscale Chinese food in swank settings, Mott 32 will slot into the site previously occupied by Silks, which closed in March. Inside Mott 32's clubby Hong Kong dining room. Named after the address of the first Chinese grocery in New York (32 Mott Street), the brand launched in 2014 in a bank tower in Hong Kong’s Central neighbourhood. There are now nine around the world, including Vancouver, Dubai and Las Vegas, with a pipeline of nine more locations including other Australian cities. Mott 32’s parent company Maximal Concepts was co-founded by entrepreneur, filmmaker and extreme sports adventurer Malcolm Wood.



“Melbourne’s a great city,” he says in the first interview he’s done about the push into Australia. “You’ve got a lot of tourism coming through, you’re multicultural, there’s a large Asian community, and you’re very well-educated about food – let’s call it culinary intelligence.” Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up Even so, he believes Mott 32 will be something new for the city. “People haven’t seen Chinese cuisine presented in such a way, with a beautiful design that competes against all the other restaurants in the city.” The restaurant ages duck for 42 days before smoking and roasting each bird. Excellent cocktails, glamorous clubby design and theatrical flourishes are Mott 32 signatures, as are modern and technically challenging versions of Chinese classics. Siu mai dumplings are made with truffled Iberico pork and soft-boiled quail egg. That smoked, roasted duck (used across several dishes) is known for its glossy, crunchy skin and tableside carving. Born in Taiwan to a Chinese mother and English father, Wood is keen to differentiate Mott 32 from other international luxury brands such as Nobu (a Crown tenant since 2007) and Zuma, with more than 30 locations worldwide. Both serve Asian cuisine but were founded in New York and London, respectively.



“We pride ourselves in being from Asia,” says Wood. “And we are one of the few international restaurants in our segment that you’ll find Asian consumers wanting to go to.” Wood’s films focus on environmental challenges. The Last Glacier is about climate change, A Plastic Ocean investigates waste. How does he parlay that into a global hospitality business? “We teach ourselves about a problem, we drive awareness through a film, and then we try to change our business off the back of it,” he says. An artist's illustration of the entry to the Melbourne restaurant. He points to an egg initiative in Hong Kong, whereby the business set up its own cage-free organic egg farm that runs off solar to avoid having to import such eggs from Europe. “[Now] we’re one of the largest suppliers of eggs in Hong Kong.” At the same time, he admits hospitality has a long way to go.

World.title: Collaborative approach needed to fix the mental health crisis for young people - Youthline
World.content:
Photo: Public Health Summer School - Otago University

Youthline says it is undertaking an average of three emergency interventions a day, up from one a week five years ago.

On Wednesday, the helpline released a new report that found young people are facing a perfect storm of mental health distress, rising living costs and digital pressures.

The State of the Generation report interviewed 1041 young people from across Aotearoa aged 12-24.

Chief executive Shae Ronald told Nine to Noon it ensured diversity was represented in the survey - wanting to "deep dive" into under-served communities.

Ronald said Youthline wanted to find out the challenges diverse groups - such as the rainbow community and neurodiverse communities - were facing and how they could be supported.

The report's findings were in line with what the helpline was hearing from callers, she said.

While mental health remained the top concern for nearly 60 percent of respondents, many felt the system was failing them due to long wait times, high costs, and a significant lack of awareness regarding available support services.

Photo: Supplied

A concerning factor, Ronald said, was that 40 percent of respondents didn't know that mental health services were available to them at any time of day.

A public campaign may be needed to ensure youth know they didn't have to go through hard times alone, she said.

Financial anxiety was a major driver of stress, with nearly half of younger teens worried about their parents' finances and older youth struggling with a difficult job market and cost of living pressure.

Ronald said Youthline was seeing increasingly complex cases, with emergency interventions jumping from one a week to more than 20 in just five years.

Callers were also getting younger - with 10 percent of all calls now coming from children under the age of 12, she said.

Improving the situation for young people in New Zealand had to be done with their input, Ronald said.

When it came to young people using social media, Ronald said a "nuanced approach" was needed and platforms needed to ensure being online was safe for them.

This included enabling safety features and removing harmful content proactively.

Any approach in improving social media for young people needed their input to ensure solutions were meaningful.

This went for any approach to improving the "youth mental health crisis", Ronald said.

Systems needed to be co-designed with youth, early intervention was needed, and programmes should be developed for schools.

Ronald didn't believe that there was no money to fix the issues in the system.

"We will pay as a society if we take that approach."

She said she had hope that Aotearoa would pay attention to what young people were saying and work together to strengthen and develop a system that works better for them.

Where to get help:

If it is an emergency and you feel like you or someone else is at risk, call 111.

World.title: What is the English Language Bill and what would it actually do in New Zealand?
World.content:
Photo: VNP / Phil Smith

Explainer - You're reading this in English right now - but should English be an official language? Parliament is soon set to decide.

A long-running debate on the status of the most commonly spoken language in New Zealand is nearing its climax in Parliament, as the English Language Act works its way through the House.

During a fiery debate in Parliament back in February at the first reading, New Zealand First leader Winston Peters made his case for the bill while many opposition MPs firmly denounced it.

Peters called it a "common sense idea" and has said it fills an anomaly where Māori and English Sign Language are already both codified as official languages in New Zealand, but English is not specifically.

Others disagree. "Language is being used as a political football here," said Dr Sharon Harvey, an associate professor specialising in applied linguistics at Auckland University of Technology.

The bill is currently before select committee with a report due to be presented on 3 September. The next step is a second reading of the bill and it's likely it would come to a final vote before November's election.

But what would the bill actually do? Here's what you need to know.

What does the bill say?

Bills are often pretty darned long, but this one can actually be summed up right here - it's only five lines.

It calls for Parliament to enact the English Language Act 2025, and says, "The purpose of this Act is to provide legislative recognition of the status of English as an official language of New Zealand" and that the Act would bind the Crown.

That's it.

Want more? Read the full bill here: English Language Bill

Photo: Waka Kotahi

What would the bill actually do?

"The bill is so short because it doesn't actually have any legal effect that needs spelt out in detail," University of Otago law professor Andrew Geddis said. "It will have literally no practical consequences at all.

"That isn't an exaggeration - it will change absolutely no aspect of Aotearoa New Zealand's current legal rules, practices or procedures. It's the linguistic equivalent of passing an Act of Parliament that says: 'The official colour of the New Zealand Rugby Team's home jersey is black.'"

The bill doesn't lay out any instructions, punishments or restrictions on other languages. It would add English as an official language alongside Te Reo Māori - which was designated in the Māori Language Act in 1987 - and English Sign Language, designated in the New Zealand Sign Language Act of 2006.

"While the bill is pretty slim in terms of its content it does serve symbolically at least to cast in legislation the pre-eminence of the already dominant and majoritarian language of NZ: English," Harvey said.

Legislatively, it would not affect Māori and ESL, Geddis said, as they have "separately guaranteed (but limited) rights to use those languages".

"Legislative language recognition was hard won for both Māori and the deaf community and so the English Language Bill also minimises the historical and contemporaneous importance of those difficult and long language struggles," Harvey said.

As written, the bill wouldn't even affect, for instance, signs that include Chinese language at some popular tourist spots, Geddis said.

"That legislative recognition does not add anything to English's existing legal role and usage. You can use English for any official, public business now. If this bill passes, you will continue to be able to do so. Nothing will have changed."

Watch: Winston Peters introduces the English Language Act.

If nothing will change, why was this bill introduced?

Making English an official language was part of the coalition agreement between National, NZ First and ACT back in 2023.

Former NZ First MP Clayton Mitchell put forth a similar member's bill in 2018 but it was never drawn from the ballot.

New Zealand First has pushed for such recognition for some time.

Did you know that English is not an official language? Well, we're changing that by delivering on a key campaign promise - we are making English an official language of New Zealand. We will continue to fight for common sense ideas and work in the interests of all New Zealanders. pic.twitter.com/ki3dDh8tDI — New Zealand First (@nzfirst) December 14, 2023

In introducing the current bill, Peters said that it's correcting an "anomaly" that English is not included with the other two official languages.

"It has never been formally recognised in statute as an official language. This bill seeks to correct that anomaly, providing consistency in legal framework and clarifying the status of all three official languages in legislation.

"The bill does not diminish the status of other official languages, te reo Māori and New Zealand Sign Language, but rather complements them, acknowledging the linguistic reality of our nation."

Peters said the bill is "affirming the value of English as a shared means of communication used by the mass majority of the population - I'll say it again quietly: used by the mass majority of the population."

Although his name is actually on the bill as the MP in charge, Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith previously told RNZ that it wasn't a top priority for National and did not speak at the first reading.

"It wouldn't be the top priority for us, absolutely not. But it's something in the coalition and it's getting done."

Peters has said that the rise in te reo Māori has "has created situations that encourage misunderstanding and confusion for all, and all for the purpose to push a narrative".

"We have some very real situations now where communications and names of important services are using te reo as primary names and language, and the room for confusion and miscommunication is huge."

Photo: Supplied / NZME

He cited the possibility of confusion where places have had primary names in Māori.

"First responders, on their vehicles and in communications, being unable to get to places because they don't know where they're going; transport services with important road signs - they have all announced that."

Harvey disagreed, saying the dynamic of Māori and English is what makes New Zealand special.

"Te reo Māori only exists in ANZ and so if it does not survive and flourish here it will not survive."

"Most of us would recognise that Te Whatu Ora means health especially if it's heading a letter with health information or is signage on a public hospital," she said.

"There is no 'danger' to English now or in the future. Apart from anything else it is the pre-eminent global language.

"It would be so much better for NZ if we could all gain high proficiency in te reo Māori (as well as English) and if schools could be proactive in supporting students' home languages, as well as teaching a variety of languages."

Is English language use becoming a "culture war" issue?

Well, people on both sides of the debate of the current bill have accused the other of "virtue signalling."

In Parliament, Peters said that "This bill won't solve the push of this virtue signalling narrative completely, but it is the first step towards ensuring logic and common sense prevails when the vast majority of New Zealanders communicate in English and understand English in a country that should use English as its primary and official language."

"The (bill) is virtue signalling to a small, monolingual in English, sector of the voting public by NZ First," Harvey said. "It's a waste of public money and time and should never have been agreed to as part of the National-NZ First coalition agreement."

Debate at the first reading was equally heated.

Photo: RNZ/Samuel Rillstone

"The English language is not under threat," said Green Party co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick. "We are literally speaking it and debating in it right now. This is a bill which is an answer to a problem that does not exist."

"The government wants to stoke a fight between te iwi Māori and Pākehā, and they want that fight to be the focus of this election," she claimed.

At the debate, National MP Rima Nakhle called for calmer temperatures.

"We're only making English official. It's not the end of the world."

Geddis said "the bill seems to be motivated by an odd form of linguistic jealousy - something akin to 'it's not fair that those languages get called official in a statute, but English doesn't!'"

New Zealand First's 2023 coalition agreement with National also stipulated that public service departments have their primary name in English and be required to communicate "primarily in English" except for entities specifically related to Māori. It has been seen in changes to how agencies such as the New Zealand Transport Agency or Health New Zealand are referred to.

Peters has also been vocal about the use of "Aotearoa" to refer to New Zealand by other MPs.

Other countries like Australia and the United Kingdom do not have any official laws on the books declaring English an official language, although it has de facto official status in government, courts and education.
